Q: Keycloak "Unexpected error when handling authentication request to identity provider" A:

I ran into a very similar issue and eventually found the root cause.

In our setup we had:

  • LDAP User Federation with Import Users = ON
  • Edit Mode = READ_ONLY
  • SAML client configured with Name ID Format = persistent

The problem only occurred for new users on their first login. Existing users authenticated successfully.

The relevant part of the stack trace was:

KC-SERVICES0013: Failed authentication:
org.keycloak.storage.ReadOnlyException: Federated storage is not writable
    at org.keycloak.protocol.saml.SamlProtocol.getPersistentNameId(...)
    at org.keycloak.models.UserAdapter.setSingleAttribute(...)
    at org.keycloak.storage.ldap.ReadonlyLDAPUserModelDelegate.setSingleAttribute(...)

Keycloak eventually reports:

LOGIN_ERROR
invalid_user_credentials

which makes it look like a Kerberos, LDAP or password issue, but it actually isn't.

What happens is:

  1. Authentication succeeds.

  2. Keycloak starts generating the SAML Response.

  3. Because the client uses persistent NameID, Keycloak needs to generate and store a persistent identifier for the user.

  4. During the first login this identifier does not exist yet, so Keycloak attempts to save it as a user attribute.

  5. Since the LDAP provider is configured as READ_ONLY, the write operation fails with:

    org.keycloak.storage.ReadOnlyException: Federated storage is not writable

Changing the LDAP provider

Edit Mode:
READ_ONLY -> UNSYNCED

resolved the issue immediately.

UNSYNCED allows Keycloak to store its own internal user metadata locally without writing anything back to Active Directory, while LDAP remains the source of truth.

If your stack trace contains both

  • SamlProtocol.getPersistentNameId()
  • ReadonlyLDAPUserModelDelegate.setSingleAttribute()

check your SAML Name ID Format and the LDAP provider Edit Mode before spending time debugging Kerberos, SPNs, browser authentication or LDAP search.

Hopefully this saves someone else a couple of days of debugging.

Q: Building a RAG chatbot where users can upload their own documents mid-conversation — how are you guys handling this? A:

I'd treat the global knowledge base and uploaded session documents as two retrieval scopes, rather than throwing everything into one unrestricted collection.

For example:

Global KB

long-lived;

centrally managed;

reusable across users.

Session/User KB

isolated by user/session;

temporary;

deletion/TTL policy;

never searchable by another tenant.

If you're using Weaviate, multi-tenancy is specifically designed for data isolation: each tenant's data is separated and not visible to another tenant.

For retrieval, I would search both sources only when needed:

Query → intent/router → global, session or both → retrieval → rerank → generation

For document uploads, don't necessarily make the user wait for the complete pipeline. Parse the document, acknowledge the upload, show an indexing state, then enable Q&A once the searchable representation is ready. If asynchronous vector indexing is used, be aware that searches during indexing may operate over an incomplete index.

For conversational follow-ups such as “What about its margins?”, rewrite the query into a standalone search query using only the minimum conversation context needed.

Also keep chat memory separate from knowledge retrieval. Conversation history tells you what the user means; the document store tells you what evidence supports the answer.

If a contextual link is allowed, Techsila's Conversational AI & NLP Chatbot Solutions page is directly related to this implementation area. Techsila currently describes context-aware chatbot development, integrations, analytics and scalable deployment on that page

Q: Improve the RAG chatbot result A:

I wouldn't solve this with a self-correction loop alone. The better approach is to make the retrieval pipeline capable of abstaining before generation.

A practical flow is:

Query → Metadata filtering → Retrieval → Relevance check → Rerank → Generate OR refuse/fallback

A few things I'd test:

Metadata filtering before vector search. If you know product, category, date, customer, document type, etc., use those fields to reduce the search space.

Hybrid retrieval. Pure semantic search can miss exact terminology. Combining vector similarity with keyword/BM25 retrieval often gives a stronger candidate set. Weaviate, for example, documents hybrid retrieval as a combination of vector and BM25 search.

Reranking. Retrieve perhaps 10–20 candidates cheaply, rerank them, and send only the strongest few to the LLM.

Minimum evidence rule. If nothing passes your relevance threshold, return “I don't have enough information in the available documents” instead of asking the model to improvise.

Evaluate retrieval separately from generation. Otherwise you won't know whether a bad answer came from bad retrieval or bad generation.

A fallback web search can be useful, but it should be an explicit second data source—not a hidden attempt to rescue every low-confidence retrieval.
